message.content:
With RF2, every extent has two copies on two different nodes. When one of three nodes fails, extents that had a copy there drop to a single live copy, so part of the data is temporarily unprotected. Nothing is lost: the surviving copy is readable, the cluster keeps serving I/O, and VMs from the failed node restart on the other two via HA if CPU and memory allow.

The cluster can partly self-heal. Curator and Stargate detect the missing replicas and rebuild second copies on the two remaining nodes, restoring two copies of all data, provided enough free capacity exists. This is why Nutanix recommends sizing for N+1.

What it cannot restore is full fault tolerance. Three nodes is the minimum for RF2, and the metadata ring (Cassandra) and Zookeeper cannot shrink below that. The two-node cluster can tolerate another disk failure but not another node failure, which would break quorum and make data unavailable even where a copy survives. Repair or replace the node to return to normal resilience.

members.label: Response D
members.answer:
With RF2, every extent of data has two copies on two different nodes. When one of three nodes fails, some extents temporarily have only one live copy, so the cluster is in a degraded, non-redundant state for that data. Data remains fully available because the surviving copy is readable, and VMs from the failed node restart on the remaining two nodes via HA, assuming enough spare CPU and memory.

The cluster can self-heal. Stargate/Curator detect the missing replicas and rebuild second copies on the two surviving nodes, restoring RF2 as long as there is enough free capacity to hold the extra copies. This is why Nutanix recommends sizing for N+1 capacity. Once the rebuild completes, the cluster tolerates another disk failure, but not another full node failure, since with two nodes the metadata quorum and RF2 placement cannot survive losing one more. Replace the node to return to full resilience.

members.label: Response C
members.answer:
RF2 normally keeps two copies of each data block on different nodes. When one node fails, blocks that had a copy on that node temporarily have **only one surviving copy**. Blocks whose copies were on the two surviving nodes still have both. A single node failure therefore does not, by itself, cause data loss, and the surviving cluster can continue serving data.

Nutanix can automatically re-replicate affected data onto the two surviving nodes, **provided sufficient usable capacity remains**, restoring two copies of those blocks. However, restoring data copies is not the same as restoring full cluster fault tolerance: the cluster is below the normal three-node minimum for RF2, and another node failure can break metadata/control-plane quorum and make data unavailable—even where a physical copy survives.

The failed node must be recovered or replaced to restore normal three-node resilience. Thus, “RF2 tolerates one node failure” does not mean the degraded cluster can safely tolerate another.

members.label: Response B
members.answer:
In a three-node Nutanix cluster with Replication Factor 2 (RF2), every piece of data and metadata has two copies stored on separate nodes. 

When one node fails, the cluster continues to operate and serve I/O without downtime, as the surviving copy of the failed node's data exists on the remaining two nodes. However, the data redundancy for the affected blocks drops to RF1 (a single point of failure). 

Unlike larger clusters, a three-node cluster **cannot** self-heal and rebuild the lost data to restore RF2 redundancy. Nutanix architecture requires a minimum of three active nodes to maintain RF2. This is not only for data placement rules but critically for the cluster's metadata (Cassandra) and configuration (Zookeeper) components, which rely on a strict quorum. 

With only two nodes remaining, the cluster lacks the required fault domains to safely rebuild. The cluster will remain in a highly vulnerable, degraded state until the failed node is repaired or a replacement node is added.

members.label: Response A
members.answer:
In a Nutanix cluster each data block is stored on **two different nodes** when the cluster is configured with **RF‑2 (Replication Factor 2)**. With three nodes, every block normally has one copy on two of the three hosts, so the cluster can tolerate the loss of a single node while still keeping **two copies for the majority of the data**.

When one node fails:

* The remaining two nodes still hold **one copy of every block** (the copy that was on the surviving node).  
* Any blocks whose *second* replica was also on the failed node lose that replica, so those blocks are temporarily **under‑replicated** (only a single copy exists).  
* The cluster marks the failed host as *down* and automatically starts a **repair/re‑balance operation**. It creates a new second replica of each under‑replicated block on the surviving nodes (or on a spare node if one exists) until RF‑2 is restored everywhere.

Thus, data redundancy drops to a **degraded state** (some blocks have only one copy) but the cluster remains **online and functional**. It will **re‑build the missing replicas** in the background, regaining full redundancy once the rebuild finishes, provided there is enough free capacity on the remaining nodes. If capacity is insufficient, the cluster stays in a degraded alert state and admin intervention is required.
